Situation1: They send an occasional text to check in with their parents over the weekend.
Expectation2: Support individuals or groups in accessing essential services and resources
Situation2: They assist someone who is struggling with paperwork or procedures needed to receive public support.
Story: My phone buzzes with a message from Mom: “Hope you’re having a good weekend. Miss you!” I glance at the clock—already past noon on Sunday. I haven’t called home all week, and guilt prickles at me. I know how much it means to my parents when I check in, even if it’s just a quick hello. But right now, I’m sitting across from Mrs. Lee at the community center, her hands trembling as she tries to fill out the forms for housing assistance. She looks at me, eyes wide with worry, and I know she’s counting on me to help her navigate this maze of paperwork. My phone vibrates again, another message from Dad this time. I feel torn—my parents expect me to be present, to show I care, but Mrs. Lee needs me to be focused and patient, to advocate for her when she feels lost. My heart aches as I stare at my phone, caught between the pull of family and the responsibility I feel toward those who rely on me.
